notes.key_messages:  Plotted points on a grid should be clearly visible, e.g. crosses. Smooth line graphs should be curves with no straight-line sections drawn with a ruler.  Observations are those which you can see. For example, ‘fizzing, bubbles or effervescence’ is an observation; ‘a gas or carbon dioxide was given off’ is not.  Candidates should avoid giving lists of answers, as an incorrect response can contradict a correct one. For example, if the correct answer is ‘precipitate dissolves’ and a candidate writes ‘precipitate dissolves and a white solid forms’, no mark can be awarded.  In the planning question, Question 4, there is no need to write a list of apparatus at the start of the answer, any apparatus used should be referred to in the description of the experiment so that it is clear for what purpose that apparatus has been used.
notes.general_comments: The vast majority of candidates successfully attempted all of the questions. Candidates found the last question, Question 4, challenging. The majority of candidates were able to complete tables of results from readings on diagrams, as in
notes.1a: Some candidates had difficulty identifying the burette. Pipette, funnel and measuring tube were common incorrect answers.
notes.1b: Methyl orange, phenolphthalein and litmus gained credit. Universal Indicator is not suitable for use in titrations.
notes.1ci: This was generally well-answered with most candidates identifying the anomalous point.
notes.1cii: Many answers were vague referring to human error, misreading the burette or parallax errors. Credit was awarded for difficulties in judging the end point and consequent overshooting. Using too much sodium hydroxide was a high-level response.
notes.1ciii: Some candidates were able to calculate the average volume of nitric acid and give their answer to an appropriate number of decimal places.
notes.1d: Marks were awarded for realising that less acid was used and therefore the acid was more concentrated. Confused answers were common. Descriptions of a displacement reaction showed a lack of knowledge and understanding. Some candidates stated that the nitric acid must be less concentrated as it was called ‘dilute nitric acid’.
notes.2a: The table of results was often completed correctly. A common error was completing the volume for Experiment 1, suggesting candidates may not have read through the experiment details carefully. Errors were also seen recording the times for Experiments 4 and 5 leaving the time in minutes and seconds or just recording the seconds and ignoring the minutes.
notes.2b: Most candidates plotted the points correctly but often not clearly. Poorly drawn line graphs were 3 3 evident, without a smooth curve. The section between 10cm and 30cm proved challenging, with some candidates drawing a straight line with a ruler. Others drew a curve with a point of inflection and so had the curve becoming less steep to the left rather than steeper.
notes.2ci: Candidates should be encouraged to show clear construction lines on the graph and ensure that these lines are parallel to the axes. A significant number of candidates did not show clearly on the grid how they worked out their answer.
notes.2cii: The question asked for a calculation and marks were lost for leaving the answer as a fraction. Incorrectly rounded numbers could not be awarded credit.
notes.2di: A few candidates confused rate and time and so incorrectly stated Experiment 5 as it had the longest time.
notes.2dii: Good responses referred to the presence of more particles and hence more frequent collisions between the particles. A lack of understanding was seen with many candidates suggesting that at higher concentration the particles had more energy or that more collisions released more energy.
notes.2e: Many candidates gave a burette or pipette. Some candidates did not read the question and stated that a measuring cylinder is more accurate than a measuring cylinder.
notes.2f: The difference to the results caused by using a smaller conical flask was only realised by better performing candidates. Many candidates thought the concentration or pressure of the reactants would increase and the rate of reaction would increase. Candidates who have done this sort of experiment should be familiar with how changing the reaction vessel will change the results obtained. In this case a greater depth of reacting mixture would lead to the cross disappearing from view in shorter times.
notes.2g: A common mistake was to join their sketch line to their plotted line so having decided the reaction would be slower they then showed the reaction slower most of the time but having the same rate at the highest or lowest concentration.
notes.3a: The majority correctly identified hydrogen as the gas given off in test 2. Responses indicated that some candidates found this challenging.
notes.3b: Solution A was often identified as an acid but many did not use the result of test 3 to identify sulfate ions.
notes.3c: Candidates were required to realise that the gas produced was carbon dioxide and then give the test for carbon dioxide. Blue litmus is not an appropriate test since candidates should know that there are other acidic gases. Similarly the use of a lighted splint is not appropriate. The fact that the splint goes out tells us that the gas does not support combustion and is not flammable – the same result is obtained with nitrogen and ammonia.
notes.3di: The expected observation was white precipitate formed. Many responses mixed up this test with the nitrate ion test and produced ammonia despite no aluminium being added and the mixture not being heated.
notes.3dii: The precipitate dissolving was known by most candidates.
notes.3ei: The expected observation was that a white precipitate formed.
notes.3eii: The precipitate dissolving was known by most candidates.
